name: The Eddington Limit
statement: A star or accreting object can shine only so brightly before its own light blows its outer layers away.
statementAccent: before its own light blows its outer layers away
meaning: The Eddington limit is the maximum luminosity a body can sustain when the outward push of its own radiation pressure just balances the inward pull of gravity. Shine any brighter and radiation pressure overwhelms gravity, driving the outer layers of a star outward or halting the infall of matter onto a compact object. Named for Arthur Eddington and worked out in the study of stellar structure, the limit is proportional to mass, so more massive objects can be more luminous. It sets a natural ceiling on the brightness of stars and on how fast black holes and neutron stars can swallow matter and grow.
mechanism: The balance is between two forces acting on an ionised gas. Radiation pressure acts mainly on the electrons, which scatter photons efficiently through Thomson scattering, while gravity acts mainly on the far heavier protons; the two species are locked together by electrical forces, so the plasma responds as a whole. Setting the outward radiation force equal to the inward gravitational force gives a luminosity proportional to the mass, about 1.26 times ten to the thirty-first watts for each solar mass, or equivalently some thirty thousand times the Sun's luminosity per solar mass. Above this luminosity, radiation wins and matter is expelled or prevented from accreting.

examples.text: The most massive, luminous stars sit near their Eddington limit and shed mass in powerful winds and outbursts, because their radiation is close to overpowering their own gravity.
The limit caps the steady rate at which a black hole or neutron star can accrete, since radiation from infalling matter pushes back, constraining how fast supermassive black holes can grow.
Some X-ray sources appear to shine above the limit for their mass, the super-Eddington puzzle, explained by beamed or non-spherical accretion rather than a violation of the physics.

variants.name: Super-Eddington accretion
variants.text: Regimes in which the apparent luminosity exceeds the classical limit through non-spherical geometry, beaming, or photon trapping in thick accretion flows, rather than a true breach of the balance.

variants.name: Opacity dependence
variants.text: The classical limit assumes electron scattering dominates the opacity; heavier elements and line opacity can lower the effective limit for real, chemically enriched gas.

whyItMatters: The Eddington limit is a fundamental ceiling in astrophysics, setting the maximum luminosity of stars and the maximum steady rate at which compact objects can accrete and grow. It shapes the structure and mass loss of the most massive stars, governs the physics of quasars and active galactic nuclei, and constrains how quickly the supermassive black holes at galactic centres could have grown in the early universe. Wherever gravity and radiation contend, from a single star to a feeding black hole, the Eddington limit marks the balance point between them.

working.text: treat the Eddington limit as the luminosity at which outward radiation pressure just offsets inward gravity, above which matter is expelled.
expect the maximum luminosity to grow in proportion to mass, so more massive stars and black holes can be more luminous.
use the limit to bound the steady rate at which a compact object can swallow matter, since accretion light pushes infalling gas back.

limits: The classical Eddington limit assumes spherical symmetry, a steady state, and that electron, or Thomson, scattering dominates the opacity, as in fully ionised hydrogen, and these assumptions are often violated in real systems. Objects can exceed the limit transiently or through non-spherical geometry, beaming, or photon trapping, which is how ultraluminous X-ray sources shine apparently super-Eddington without breaking the physics. The exact value also depends on chemical composition, since heavier elements and line opacity change the effective opacity and lower the limit, so the simple formula is an idealisation.
misreadings: It is not an absolute cap that can never be crossed; it is the steady, spherical balance point, and transient or geometrically beamed sources genuinely exceed it in apparent luminosity. The limit depends on mass, not on the object's radius, which cancels because both forces fall off with the square of distance. And although the proton mass appears in the formula, the relevant cross-section is the electron's, reflecting that electrons scatter the radiation while protons carry the weight.
origin: Developed by Arthur Eddington in his work on the internal structure of stars in the 1920s, notably in his 1926 'The Internal Constitution of the Stars'.
